title: VII. “It’s Always Worth While Speaking To A Clever Man”
paragraphs: And in that same nervous frenzy he spoke. Meeting Fyodor Pavlovitch in the drawing room the moment he went in, he shouted at him, waving his hands, “I'm going upstairs to my room, not in to you. Good-bye!” and passed by, trying not even to look at his father. Very possibly the old man was too hateful to him at that moment; but such an unceremonious display of hostility was a surprise even to Fyodor Pavlovitch. And the old man had evidently wanted to tell him something right away and had come out to meet him in the drawing room on purpose. Greeted like that, he stood still in silence, and with an ironical air watched his son going upstairs, until he passed out of sight.
“What's the matter with him?” he promptly asked Smerdyakov, who had followed Ivan.
“Angry about something. Who can tell?” the valet muttered evasively.
“Confound him! Let him be angry then. Bring in the samovar, and get along with you. Look sharp! No news?”

Then followed a series of questions such as Smerdyakov had just complained of to Ivan, all relating to his expected visitor, which we will leave out. Half an hour later the house was locked up, and the crazy old man was wandering through the rooms in excited expectation of hearing every minute the five knocks they had agreed on. Now and then he peered out into the darkness, seeing nothing.

It was very late, but Ivan was still awake and thinking. He sat up late that night, until two o'clock. But we won't give an account of his thoughts, and this isn't the place to look into that soul — its turn will come. And even if one tried, it would be very hard to give an account of them, for there weren't really thoughts in his brain, but something very vague — and, above all, intense excitement. He felt himself that he had lost his bearings. He was fretted, too, by all sorts of strange and almost surprising desires; for instance, after midnight he was suddenly gripped by an intense, irresistible urge to go downstairs, open the door, go to the lodge and beat Smerdyakov. But if he'd been asked why, he couldn't have given any exact reason, except perhaps that he loathed the valet as someone who had insulted him more grievously than anyone else in the world. On the other hand, he was more than once that night overcome by a sort of inexplicable, humiliating terror that he felt positively paralyzed his physical powers. His head ached and he was dizzy. A feeling of hatred rankled in his heart, as though he meant to take revenge on someone. He even hated Alyosha, remembering the conversation they'd just had. At moments he hated himself intensely. He almost forgot to think about Katerina Ivanovna, and wondered greatly at that afterward, especially as he remembered perfectly how, when he'd been so valiantly protesting to Katerina Ivanovna that he'd be leaving next day for Moscow, something had whispered in his heart, “That's nonsense, you're not going, and it won't be so easy to tear yourself away as you're boasting now.”

Remembering that night long afterward, Ivan recalled with peculiar revulsion how he had suddenly got up from the sofa and had stealthily, as though afraid of being watched, opened the door, gone out onto the staircase, and listened to Fyodor Pavlovitch stirring down below; he had listened a long while — some five minutes — with a sort of strange curiosity, holding his breath while his heart throbbed. And why he'd done all this, why he was listening, he couldn't have said. That “action” he forever afterward called “infamous,” and in the bottom of his heart he thought of it as the basest action of his life. For Fyodor Pavlovitch himself he felt no hatred at that moment, but was simply intensely curious to know how he was walking around down there, and what he must be doing now. He wondered and imagined how he must be peeping out of the dark windows and stopping in the middle of the room, listening, listening — for someone to knock. Ivan went out onto the stairs twice to listen like that.

Around two o'clock, when everything was quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan got into bed firmly resolved to fall asleep at once, as he felt fearfully exhausted. And he did fall asleep at once, and slept soundly without dreams, but woke early, at seven, when it was broad daylight. Opening his eyes, he was surprised to feel himself extraordinarily vigorous. He jumped up at once and dressed quickly; then dragged out his trunk and started packing straight away. His linen had come back from the laundress the previous morning. Ivan actually smiled at the thought that everything was helping his sudden departure. And his departure certainly was sudden. Though Ivan had said the day before (to Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha, and Smerdyakov) that he was leaving the next day, he remembered that he'd had no thought of leaving when he went to bed — or at any rate, had not dreamed that his first act in the morning would be to pack his trunk. At last his trunk and bag were ready. It was about nine o'clock when Marfa Ignatyevna came in with her usual inquiry: “Where will your honor take your tea — in your own room or downstairs?” He looked almost cheerful, but there was something about him, about his words and gestures, that was hurried and scattered. Greeting his father amiably, and even inquiring specially after his health — though he didn't wait to hear his answer to the end — he announced that he was setting off in an hour to return to Moscow for good, and asked him to send for the horses. His father heard this announcement with no sign of surprise, and forgot in an unmannerly way to show regret at losing him. Instead, he flew into a great flutter at the recollection of some important business of his own.

“What a fellow you are! Not to tell me yesterday! Never mind — we'll manage it all the same. Do me a great service, my dear boy. Stop by Tchermashnya on the way. It's just a left turn from the station at Volovya — only another twelve versts and you come to Tchermashnya.”
“I'm sorry, I can't. It's eighty versts to the railway, and the train leaves for Moscow at seven o'clock tonight. I can only just catch it.”

“You'll catch it tomorrow or the day after — but today turn off to Tchermashnya. It won't put you out much to humor your father! If I hadn't had something to keep me here, I'd have run over myself long ago, because I've some urgent business there. But here I ... this isn't the time for me to go.... You see, I have two plots of copse land there. The Maslovs, an old merchant and his son, will give eight thousand for the timber. But last year I just missed a buyer who would have given twelve. There's no finding anyone around here to buy it. The Maslovs have it all their own way. One has to take what they'll give, because no one around here dares bid against them. The priest at Ilyinskoe wrote to me last Thursday that a merchant called Gorstkin, a man I know, had turned up. What makes him valuable is that he's not from these parts, so he's not afraid of the Maslovs. He says he'll give me eleven thousand for the copse. Do you hear? But, the priest writes, he'll only be here for a week altogether, so you have to go at once and strike a bargain with him.”
“Well, write to the priest then; he'll make the bargain.”

“He can't do it. He has no eye for business. He's a perfect treasure, I'd give him twenty thousand to look after for me without a receipt — but he has no eye for business, he's a perfect child, a crow could deceive him. And yet he's a learned man, would you believe it? This Gorstkin looks like a peasant — he wears a blue kaftan — but he's a regular rogue. That's the common complaint. He's a liar. Sometimes he tells such lies that you wonder why he's doing it. He told me the year before last that his wife had died and that he'd married another, and would you believe it, there wasn't a word of truth in it? His wife has never died at all; she's alive to this day and gives him a beating twice a week. So what you have to find out is whether he's lying or telling the truth when he says he wants to buy it and would give eleven thousand.”
“I'd be no use in such a business. I have no eye for it either.”

“Wait, wait a bit! You'll be useful, because I'll tell you the signs by which you can judge Gorstkin. I've done business with him a long time. You see, you have to watch his beard; he has a nasty, thin, red beard. If his beard shakes when he talks, and he gets cross, then it's all right, he means what he says, he wants to do business. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins — he's trying to cheat you. Don't watch his eyes, you won't learn anything from his eyes, he's a deep one, a rogue — but watch his beard! I'll give you a note to show him. He's called Gorstkin, though his real name is Lyagavy;[4] but don't call him that, he'll be offended. If you come to an understanding with him and see it's all right, write here at once. You only have to write: ‘He's not lying.’ Hold out for eleven thousand; you can knock off one thousand, but no more. Just think! there's a difference between eight thousand and eleven thousand. It's as good as picking up three thousand; it's not so easy to find a purchaser, and I'm in desperate need of money. Just let me know it's serious, and I'll run over and fix it up. I'll snatch the time somehow. But what's the good of my galloping over if it's all some notion of the priest's? Come, will you go?”
“Oh, I can't spare the time. You'll have to excuse me.”

“Come, you might oblige your father. I won't forget it. You've got no heart, any of you — that's the truth! What's a day or two to you? Where are you off to now — Venice? Your Venice will still be there in two more days. I'd have sent Alyosha, but what use is Alyosha in a thing like this? I'm sending you precisely because you're a clever fellow. Do you think I don't see that? You know nothing about timber, but you've got an eye. All that's needed is to see whether the man's in earnest. I tell you, watch his beard — if his beard shakes, you know he's in earnest.”
“You're forcing me to go to that damned Tchermashnya yourself, then?” Ivan cried, with a malignant smile.
Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't catch, or wouldn't catch, the malignancy, but he caught the smile.
“Then you'll go, you'll go? I'll scribble the note for you at once.”
“I don't know whether I'll go. I don't know. I'll decide on the way.”

“Nonsense! Decide at once. My dear fellow, decide! If you settle the matter, write me a line; give it to the priest and he'll send it on to me at once. And I won't delay you any longer than that. You can go to Venice. The priest will give you horses back to Volovya station.”

The old man was quite delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased he usually became expansive, but today he seemed to restrain himself. Of Dmitri, for instance, he didn't say a word. He was quite unmoved by the parting, and seemed, in fact, at a loss for something to say. Ivan noticed this particularly. “He must be bored with me,” he thought. Only when he was accompanying his son out onto the steps did the old man begin to fuss. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hastily held out his hand, obviously avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once, and instantly pulled himself up.
“Well, good luck to you, good luck to you!” he repeated from the steps. “You'll come back again some time or other? Mind you do come. I'll always be glad to see you. Well, Christ be with you!”
Ivan got into the carriage.
“Good-bye, Ivan! Don't be too hard on me!” his father called for the last time.
The whole household came out to take leave — Smerdyakov, Marfa, and Grigory. Ivan gave them ten roubles each. When he had seated himself in the carriage, Smerdyakov jumped up to arrange the rug.

“You see ... I'm going to Tchermashnya,” suddenly broke from Ivan. Again, as the day before, the words seemed to drop out of themselves, and he laughed, too, a peculiar, nervous laugh. He remembered it long after.
“It's a true saying, then, that ‘it's always worth while speaking to a clever man,’” Smerdyakov answered firmly, looking meaningfully at Ivan.

The carriage rolled away. Nothing was clear in Ivan's soul, but he looked eagerly around him at the fields, at the hills, at the trees, at a flock of geese flying high overhead in the bright sky. And all of a sudden he felt very happy. He tried to speak to the driver, and felt intensely interested in an answer the peasant gave him; but a minute later he realized he wasn't catching anything, and hadn't really even taken in the peasant's answer. He fell silent, and it was pleasant even so. The air was fresh, pure, and cool, the sky bright. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna floated into his mind. But he softly smiled, blew softly on the friendly phantoms, and they flew away. “There's plenty of time for them,” he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and galloped on to Volovya. “Why is it worth while speaking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?” The thought seemed to grip his breathing. “And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?” They reached Volovya station. Ivan got out of the carriage, and the drivers stood around him bargaining over the twelve-verst journey to Tchermashnya. He told them to harness the horses. He went into the station house, looked around, glanced at the overseer's wife, and suddenly went back out to the entrance.
“I won't go to Tchermashnya. Am I too late to reach the railway by seven, brothers?”
“We'll just make it. Shall we get the carriage out?”
“At once. Is any of you going to the town tomorrow?”
“Sure. Mitri here is.”
“Can you do me a service, Mitri? Go to my father's, to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, and tell him I haven't gone to Tchermashnya. Can you?”
“Of course I can. I've known Fyodor Pavlovitch a long time.”
“And here's something for you, for I dare say he won't give you anything,” Ivan said, laughing cheerfully.
“You may depend on it, he won't.” Mitya laughed too. “Thank you, sir. I'll be sure to do it.”

At seven o'clock Ivan got on the train and set off for Moscow. “Away with the past. I'm done with the old world forever, and may I have no news, no echo, from it. On to a new life, new places, and no looking back!” But instead of delight, his soul was filled with such gloom, and his heart ached with such anguish, as he had never known in his life before. He thought all night long. The train flew on, and only at daybreak, as he was approaching Moscow, did he suddenly rouse himself from his brooding.
“I am a scoundrel,” he whispered to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was quite satisfied at having seen his son off. For two hours afterward he felt almost happy, and sat drinking brandy. But suddenly something happened which was very annoying and unpleasant for everyone in the house, and immediately upset Fyodor Pavlovitch's equanimity. Smerdyakov went to the cellar for something and fell down from the top of the steps. Fortunately, Marfa Ignatyevna was in the yard and heard him in time. She didn't see the fall, but heard his scream — the strange, peculiar scream, long familiar to her — the scream of an epileptic falling in a fit. They couldn't tell whether the fit had come on him at the moment he was descending the steps, so that he must have fallen unconscious, or whether it was the fall and the shock that had caused the fit in Smerdyakov, who was known to be liable to them. They found him at the bottom of the cellar steps, writhing in convulsions and foaming at the mouth. It was thought at first that he must have broken something — an arm or a leg — and injured himself, but “God had preserved him,” as Marfa Ignatyevna put it — nothing of the kind had happened. But it was difficult to get him out of the cellar. They asked the neighbors to help, and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovitch himself was present through the whole business. He helped, evidently alarmed and upset. The sick man didn't regain consciousness; the convulsions ceased for a time, but then started again, and everyone concluded that the same thing would happen as had happened a year before, when he accidentally fell from the garret. They remembered that ice had been put on his head then. There was still ice in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna had some brought up. In the evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who arrived at once. He was a most estimable old man, and the most careful and conscientious doctor in the province. After careful examination, he concluded that the fit was a very violent one and might have serious consequences; that in the meantime he, Herzenstube, didn't fully understand it, but that by tomorrow morning, if the present remedies were unavailing, he would venture to try something else. The sick man was taken to the lodge, to a room next to Grigory and Marfa Ignatyevna's.

Then Fyodor Pavlovitch had one misfortune after another to put up with that day. Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and the soup, compared with Smerdyakov's, was “no better than dish-water,” and the fowl was so dried up it was impossible to chew. To her master's bitter, though deserved, reproaches, Marfa Ignatyevna replied that the fowl had been a very old one to begin with, and that she had never been trained as a cook. In the evening there was more trouble in store for Fyodor Pavlovitch; he was informed that Grigory, who hadn't been well for the past three days, was completely laid up by his lumbago. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea as early as possible and locked himself in the house alone. He was in terrible excitement and suspense. That evening he counted on Grushenka's coming almost as a certainty. He had received an assurance from Smerdyakov that morning “that she had promised to come without fail.” The incorrigible old man's heart throbbed with excitement; he paced up and down his empty rooms listening. He had to be on the alert. Dmitri might be on the watch for her somewhere, and when she knocked on the window (Smerdyakov had told him two days before that he'd told her where and how to knock), the door had to be opened at once. She mustn't be a second in the passage, for fear — which God forbid! — that she should be frightened and run away. Fyodor Pavlovitch had much to think about, but never had his heart been steeped in such voluptuous hopes. This time he could say almost for certain that she'd come!
